title: AI-Native Readiness Score
subtitle: Measures how far your mid-market operation is from running on agents — and where the gap is costing you the most.

questions.text: How are most AI tools used in your business right now?

answers.label: A few employees use ChatGPT on their own. Nothing about how we operate has changed.
We've bought software with AI in the marketing copy. It drafts things, but the work is the same.
Someone on ops wired up an automation between two systems. It works until something changes, then it breaks silently.
At least one real workflow runs on an agent connected to our system of record, with a human approving anything that leaves the building.
Several workflows run this way and adding new volume doesn't automatically mean a new hire.

questions.text: How does your team find out when an AI system breaks or starts producing bad output?

answers.label: We don't have AI systems running yet.
A user notices something wrong and reports it — usually after it's already caused a problem.
We check manually from time to time, but there's no system.
We have alerts for common failure cases and review exceptions before they compound.
Every agent run is logged. Exceptions trigger automatic review before anything leaves the system.

questions.text: When new volume hits — more orders, more clients, more requests — what happens first?

answers.label: We immediately think about who to hire.
Everyone works longer hours until we can bring someone on.
We try to automate something, but we usually still end up hiring.
Some workflows handle the surge, but the core still needs more people.
New volume runs through agents. Headcount stays flat.

low.headline: You're at Level 1 or 2. Most mid-market companies are.
low.text: The risk isn't where you are — it's thinking Level 2 is progress. A CRM with AI features isn't a transformed operation. It's a dressed-up manual process. The first move isn't another tool. It's identifying one workflow that runs hundreds of times a month and asking whether an agent could own it.
steps: Name the single highest-volume repetitive workflow in your business this week.
Count how many hours per week it takes across your full team.
List every way that workflow goes wrong when the input isn't clean — that list becomes the spec for the agent.

mid.headline: You've got something running. The gap is between demo and production.
mid.text: Most businesses I talk to have an automation that works until an input changes format, then breaks silently for a week. The move from Level 3 to Level 4 is one real agent, connected to your system of record, with a human approving anything that leaves the building — and built for the messy version of the input, not just the clean one.
steps: Audit the automation you have: what happens when the input format changes or a field is missing?
Add a hard gate — nothing touches a customer or money without a human clicking approve.
Log every run. You need receipts before the training wheels come off.

high.headline: You're operating above where most mid-market companies will be in three years.
high.text: The question now is whether new volume has genuinely stopped requiring new hires. If you're still adding headcount in proportion to new clients, there's still work to do. Level 5 is when capacity stops being a function of how many people you employ.
steps: Audit which workflows still scale linearly with headcount — those are the next targets.
Identify the next workflow that runs 500-plus times a month and hand it to an agent.
Set the benchmark: what does it cost to onboard a new client today, and how much of that should an agent own?

questions.text: How many total team-hours per week does your business spend on work that follows the same steps every time — copying, checking, chasing, updating, reporting?
questions.hint: Add all staff who touch this work. If 3 people each spend 4 hours on manual reporting, enter 12. For the cost estimate below, we use $60/hour as a loaded average for mid-market operations staff (salary plus benefits plus overhead for most roles in the 50–500 employee range) and 52 weeks per year.

questions.text: How clearly can you name the workflows where someone is copying, checking, moving, chasing, or updating — and that work repeats at least 50 times a month?

answers.label: I haven't mapped this yet.
I can name a few from memory, but I haven't documented them.
We've listed the main ones but haven't counted the hours they take.
We've mapped these workflows and know roughly how many weekly hours each one takes.
Fully mapped, hours quantified, and at least one already running on an agent.

questions.text: Think about your highest-volume repetitive process — order entry, reporting, follow-up, inbox triage, quote building. What's true of it today?

answers.label: It runs entirely on manual effort from the team.
We have templates or checklists, but a human drives every step.
Part of it is automated, but someone still handles every exception manually.
An agent handles the standard cases; a human reviews before anything goes out.
It runs end to end on an agent. The team steps in only when something looks off.

questions.text: How much of your team's week is work that looks the same every time — same steps, same format, same output?

answers.label: More than half of total team hours.
Roughly 40–60% of total team hours.
Around 20–40%.
Under 20% — we've automated most of the standard work.
Almost none. Routine work runs on agents; the team handles judgment calls.

low.headline: The manual work is bleeding the most time and money.
low.text: Order entry. Claims. Collections follow-up. Reporting. Inbox triage. Quote building. Work where someone is copying, checking, moving, chasing, updating. You don't fix this by buying another tool. You hand the workflow to an agent. The first step is mapping it — not automating it.
steps: List every workflow where the same steps happen at least 50 times a month.
For each one, count the weekly hours across every person who touches it.
Rank by hours times cost. The top item is where you start.

mid.headline: You can see the workflows. Now build one that runs itself.
mid.text: You know where the manual work is. The gap is between knowing and handing it to an agent. The boring workflows — the ones that run 500 times a week and never make a demo — are exactly where AI matters. This is easier in the mid-market. Workflows are smaller. Teams are closer to the work.
steps: Take your highest-hours workflow and document every step, including every way it goes wrong.
Identify which steps are deterministic — same input, same output. Those are software, not AI.
Build the agent for the judgment calls only. Let regular code handle the rest.

high.headline: Most of the manual bleeding is under control. Stay ahead of re-accumulation.
high.text: Businesses accumulate manual work the way buildings accumulate maintenance debt. Winning one workflow doesn't mean the problem stays solved. The question is whether you have a process for catching new manual accumulation before it calcifies.
steps: Run a quarterly audit: which workflows have grown in manual hours since the last review?
Set a threshold — any workflow crossing 20 team-hours per week gets evaluated for automation.
Document the agent playbook so the next one doesn't take as long to build as the first.

questions.text: When you've tested AI tools or automations with real data, what does that data typically look like?

answers.label: We haven't tested anything with real operational data yet.
We've only tested with clean, well-formatted data in controlled conditions.
We've used real data, but the system breaks when formats change or fields are missing.
We've mapped the ways inputs go wrong and built the agent to handle most of them.
Our agents treat messy, missing, and inconsistent data as the default — not an edge case.

questions.text: What happens when an AI agent in your business makes a mistake or produces a bad output?

answers.label: We don't have agents taking actions yet.
Someone catches it eventually — usually after it's already caused a problem.
We have some manual review, but it isn't systematic.
Nothing leaves the building without a human approving it — everything is gated.
Every action is logged and gated. Agents earn autonomy on specific action types as they prove reliable.

questions.text: How do you know whether an AI workflow is performing well or silently degrading?

answers.label: We don't have AI workflows running yet.
We assume it's fine unless someone complains.
We spot-check output quality when we remember.
Spot checks are built into the workflow at regular intervals.
Every run is logged. Quality drift triggers a review before it becomes a problem.

low.headline: A demo works because someone fed it clean data in a conference room. Production is different.
low.text: The agents that survive are built for the ugly stuff — missing data, formats you don't control, records that don't exist. Before you build, sit down and list every way the task goes wrong. That list is the spec. Skip it and the agent breaks on week two.
steps: Pick one workflow and write down every way the input can arrive broken, incomplete, or in an unexpected format.
Build handling for each failure mode before the agent goes live — not after.
Gate every action that touches a customer, an order, or money. Nothing leaves without a human clicking approve.

mid.headline: You have something running. Now make sure it keeps receipts.
mid.text: An agent that takes actions without a log is an agent you can't audit, fix, or trust. Every single action should be recorded. The training wheels come off as the agent earns it — not before.
steps: Audit every AI action currently running in your business: is it logged?
For any action that isn't gated, add a human-approval step now.
Define what the agent needs to demonstrate before a gate comes off. Write that criteria down.

high.headline: Your agents are built like they belong in production.
high.text: Messy input handled. Gated output. Full logs. That's the foundation. The question now is whether the next agent you build goes through the same standard — or whether the rigor only applies to the ones you personally built.
steps: Write down the production-readiness checklist you ran on your existing agents.
Apply it as a formal gate before any new agent goes live.
Review logs quarterly for silent drift — agents that worked at launch don't always stay reliable.

questions.text: If your revenue doubled tomorrow, what would you actually need to handle the volume?

answers.label: Significantly more staff — we'd need to hire across most functions.
More staff in most areas, plus some process improvement.
A few key hires and better tooling in a few areas.
Mostly tooling and process changes — minimal hiring needed.
Our operation would absorb it. Headcount stays close to flat.

questions.text: How much of your operation's quality depends on specific individuals carrying knowledge in their heads?

answers.label: Most of what we know about how to do things lives with specific people.
Some documentation exists, but critical knowledge is still personal.
Key processes are documented, but execution still relies on experienced staff.
Most processes are documented and transferable — new people can pick them up quickly.
The systems carry the knowledge. New hires or new volume don't reset the quality.

questions.text: How does your cost to deliver — per client, per order, per project — change as volume grows?

answers.label: It stays the same per unit. More volume means proportionally more cost.
We get some efficiency at scale, but more clients always means more people.
Some functions scale; others still add headcount linearly.
Most functions scale without adding people. A few still don't.
Per-unit delivery cost drops as volume grows. New clients don't automatically mean new hires.

low.headline: Your capacity is still a function of how many people you employ.
low.text: That's the ceiling. Every new client is another hire. Every new hire is another manager, another onboarding, another person who knows something nobody else does. The goal of going AI-native isn't cost-cutting. It's breaking the link between volume and headcount so you can grow without the growth tax.
steps: List the three functions where adding volume automatically means adding people.
For each one, identify the work that happens the same way every time — that's the agent candidate.
Start with the function where the hire is most expensive or hardest to find.

mid.headline: Some workflows scale. Others still pull headcount along with them.
mid.text: Most mid-market companies have automated the easy parts and left the hard ones alone. The hard ones are usually closest to customers or money — where people feel nervous about an agent running it. That nervousness is a gate problem, not a capability problem.
steps: Identify which client-facing or revenue-adjacent workflows still require dedicated people.
Build the gate first — human approval on every action — then run the agent behind it.
Measure time-to-delivery before and after. The data makes the case for removing the gate.

high.headline: New volume doesn't automatically mean a new hire. That's what Level 5 looks like.
high.text: Most companies in your space will still be adding headcount in proportion to revenue when you're running the same volume on a flat team. The question now is whether you've closed the tribal knowledge gap — when key people leave, does the quality go with them?
steps: Audit knowledge dependencies: if your three most experienced people left this month, which workflows would break?
For each one, run an SOP generation pass — extract the knowledge into a documented, agent-readable format.
Test it: can a new hire reach full output quality in under two weeks using only the system?

questions.text: When your business adopts a new AI tool or builds an automation, what does the process look like?

answers.label: An employee finds a tool they like and starts using it.
We evaluate tools and roll them out, but there's no consistent approach.
We have a rollout process, but it doesn't cover failure modes or approval gates.
We follow a structured approach: map the workflow, test with real inputs, gate approvals, log every action.
We embed AI into operations the same way every time: audit, build, gate, run, monitor.

questions.text: What does the approval structure look like for actions your AI systems take?

answers.label: We don't have AI systems taking actions yet.
Agents take actions freely — we check outcomes periodically.
We review output for important actions, but it isn't systematic.
Any action that touches a customer, an order, or money requires a human to click approve before it goes out.
Every action category has a defined gate. Agents earn autonomy on specific action types over time, and every action is logged.

low.headline: Agents without gates are a liability, not an asset.
low.text: Email a customer, commit an order, move money — none of it should happen without a human clicking approve. Day one, everything is gated. The agents that survive in real businesses have a hard NO list and they keep receipts. Without that foundation you're not building infrastructure — you're running experiments that will break at the worst moment.
steps: List every AI action currently happening in your business — every send, commit, or update.
Add a human-approval gate to each one before the next run.
Write the hard NO list: what are the actions an agent will never take without human sign-off?

mid.headline: You have gates. Now make them consistent.
mid.text: Ad hoc review is better than no review, but it doesn't scale. When the same workflow runs 500 times a week, spot checks miss more than they catch. The goal is a gate structure you can document and repeat — so every new agent starts with the same guardrails, not the ones you remember to add.
steps: Document the approval logic for your most active AI workflow: what triggers a review, who approves, and what's logged?
Standardize that into a template you apply to the next agent you build.
Set a quarterly review: which gates can come off because the agent has earned it?

high.headline: You're running infrastructure, not experiments.
high.text: Audit trail, defined gates, criteria for earning autonomy. That's what separates the agents that survive from the ones that break in production and never get rebuilt. The companies that will be fully AI-native in two years are building this structure now.
steps: Run an audit: for each agent, can you answer — what does it log, what is gated, and what has it earned autonomy on?
If any agent can't answer all three, close the gap before you add the next one.
Write the internal playbook: how does your business onboard a new agent? That document is your AI operating system.

cta.headline: Want a partner who turns this score into an actual plan?
cta.description: Most people don't fail at the assessment. They fail at sequencing. In 30 minutes I'll show you which two things to fix first, based on your score and your stage. No pitch deck, just the sequencing call.
